chapter_title: Introduction to React Native Components & JSX

screens.title: Components & JSX — Building Blocks of a React Native UI
screens.subtitle: Understand core components, JSX syntax, inline styles, and StyleSheet organization.

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn what components and JSX are, and why they are central to building React Native apps. Components are independent, reusable pieces of user interface that encapsulate rendering and behavior. That means you compose an interface from small parts like a container, text label, or image. JSX is the syntax you use to describe those parts with a familiar, H T M L-like structure inside JavaScript. You will see how View, Text, and Image map to native widgets on iOS and Android, why all textual content must be wrapped in a Text component, and how style in React Native uses JavaScript objects rather than C S S strings. We will also practice two ways to style components: inline style objects for quick adjustments, and the StyleSheet. create() pattern for better organization and performance. A short, concrete profile-card example will walk through both approaches so you can see how everything fits together. Along the way I will point out a common beginner mistake — placing raw text directly inside a View — and how to correct it. By the end you will be able to write simple JSX UIs, apply inline and extracted styles, and explain why StyleSheet helps with reuse and native-side optimization. Ready to build your first profile card and know the rules that keep it cross-platform?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Components compose UI; JSX describes them in JavaScript; styles are JavaScript objects applied via the style prop or organized with StyleSheet.create().

screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives map to concrete skills you should be able to perform. First, you will be able to explain what a component is and why components are the fundamental building blocks of a React Native UI. You should be able to say how components encapsulate rendering and behavior and provide a concrete example such as a profile-card component composed from View, Image, and Text. Second, you will learn to differentiate core components — View, Text, and Image — by their purpose and constraints. For example, understand that text must be wrapped in a Text component and why a View cannot display raw text by itself. Third, you will write basic UI structures using JSX that describe the tree of components. You should be comfortable with JSX syntax, such as self-closing tags and expression braces. Fourth, you will apply styles both inline and using StyleSheet. create(), and understand when to centralize styles for reuse and performance. Each objective includes a short example or mnemonic so you can see the skill in code and in practice.

screens.title: What is a Component?
screens.subtitle: Definition, role, and a concrete profile-card example

narration.text: A component is an independent, reusable piece of UI that encapsulates how something looks and behaves. In React Native, components can be simple presentational parts like a label or image, or they can contain logic and state. Think of a component as a small function: it takes properties and state, and returns a rendered UI tree. A practical example is a profile-card component that has a profile image, a name, and a title. That component can be reused anywhere you need to show a user summary. When you change the implementation in one place, every instance benefits. A common misconception is treating components like global templates; instead, they should be small, focused, and composable. Another misconception is assuming components are platform-specific — React Native's core components map to native widgets under the hood, but your component code can remain cross-platform. Concretely, imagine a ProfileCard that accepts a name, role, and avatar URL as props and returns a View containing an Image and two Texts. If the avatar style needs to change, update it in the component and all usages update automatically. Key takeaway: design components for reuse, test them with different prop values, and prefer small focused components over giant multitasking ones. How could you split a complex header into smaller components for clearer reuse?

keyIdea.title: Component takeaway
keyIdea.text: Components encapsulate UI and behavior; design them small, reusable, and prop-driven so they compose easily across an app.

content.html:
Core Concept

What is a Component?

A component encapsulates rendering and optional behavior. It receives props and returns UI. Components enable reuse and clearer code structure.

Why it matters
  • Promotes reuse: update one component and all instances reflect the change.
  • Improves testability: small units are easier to reason about.
  • Encourages composition: build complex UI from simple parts.
Common mistake
Create overly large components that mix unrelated concerns; prefer splitting into focused components.
ProfileCard — example component
Jane Doe
Mobile App Developer
Example props
name, role, avatarUri — pass different values to reuse the same component for different users.
Key Takeaway

Keep components focused and prop-driven so they are easy to reuse and maintain.

narration.text: React Native provides core components that map to native UI primitives. The most fundamental are View, Text, and Image. View is a flexible container similar to a web div; it provides layout, touch handling, and accessibility. Use View whenever you need to group elements or arrange layout with Flexbox. Text is specialized for rendering textual content — a critical rule is that every piece of visible text must be wrapped inside a Text component. If you place raw text directly inside a View you will get an error or unexpected layout. Image displays bitmap content from local assets or network URIs and accepts size and border properties through the style prop. A common beginner confusion is thinking that styles cascade like C S S on the web. In React Native each component receives its own style object, and styles do not cascade. Also, while a View can contain Text, Text can contain nested Text elements that inherit text-specific props like font and color in a more controlled way. Practically, choose View for layout, Text for any visible text, and Image for photos or icons. As an exercise, replace a static avatar box with an Image component and test different width/height style values to see how it behaves. What would break if you accidentally left a name as raw text inside a View?

keyIdea.title: Core components
keyIdea.text: View handles layout, Text handles all textual rendering, and Image displays images — use each for its intended purpose and avoid raw text inside Views.

content.html:
Comparison

View vs Text vs Image

View
Layout container, handles Flexbox, touch events, and accessibility. Similar to a web div but native-backed.
Text
Dedicated to displaying text. All visible text must be wrapped in Text components; nesting Text is supported.
Image
Displays images from local or remote sources. Style controls size, border radius, and layout.
Misconception
Styles cascade like web CSS — they do not. Each component's style prop is independent.
Concrete scenario
Name must be in Text
If you accidentally put raw text into a View you will lose text layout control and may see runtime warnings. Always wrap text nodes.
Key Takeaway

Respect component roles: View for layout, Text for text, Image for images. This prevents layout errors and keeps code predictable.

screens.title: JSX: JavaScript XML for UI
screens.subtitle: What JSX is, how it’s transpiled, and key differences from HTML

narration.text: JSX is a syntax extension that allows you to write H T M L-like structures directly inside JavaScript. It is not H T M L, however. Under the hood, JSX expressions are transpiled into JavaScript function calls that create the component tree. For example, a JSX element that looks like a tag actually becomes a call that describes the element type and its props. This makes JSX both expressive and familiar to developers coming from the web. Key differences you should remember: attribute names may differ to avoid reserved JavaScript keywords — for example, class becomes className on the web, and in React Native you use style as an object rather than a C S S string. You also use curly braces to evaluate JavaScript expressions inside JSX, which is how you can insert variables or conditional values. A common error is to treat JSX like a template language and attempt to place statements directly inside it. Keep control flow in JavaScript expressions and use ternaries or extracted functions to keep JSX declarative. A concrete example: embedding a user's name variable inside a Text element via braces. Finally, understand that self-closing tags are valid for components without children. After this, you'll be better equipped to read and write component trees that describe UI clearly and predictably. What expression would you use to conditionally show a subtitle only when a user has a role?

keyIdea.title: JSX rule
keyIdea.text: JSX looks like HTML but is JavaScript that gets transpiled; use braces for expressions and object style props for styling.

content.html:
Definition

JSX

A JavaScript syntax extension that represents UI structure. It reads like HTML, but it compiles to JavaScript calls that create elements and pass props.

Important rules
  • Use curly braces to evaluate JavaScript inside JSX.
  • Self-closing tags are allowed for elements without children.
  • Keep statements out of JSX; use expressions or helper functions instead.
Misconception
JSX runs in the browser the same way HTML does — it does not. It is compiled into JavaScript before execution.
Concrete example
{`// JSX snippet (visual only)

  {userName}
  {userRole ? {userRole} : null}
  
`}
Notice the braces used to insert variables and to evaluate a conditional expression. Style is passed as an object, not a CSS string.
Key Takeaway

Use JSX to declaratively express UI; keep logic in JavaScript expressions and pass styles as objects.

screens.title: Inline Styles with JavaScript Objects
screens.subtitle: How inline styles work and the meaning of double curly braces

narration.text: React Native uses JavaScript objects for styles. Inline styling is convenient for quick adjustments and dynamic values. When you see syntax like style={{ color: 'blue', fontSize: 20 }}, the outer braces denote a JavaScript expression inside JSX, and the inner braces define an object literal. Inline styles are useful when you compute values from props or state, such as setting fontSize based on a user preference. However, inline styles duplicate objects if used everywhere and can make reuse harder. A common beginner mistake is to try writing C S S strings instead of objects. Remember property names use camelCase in JavaScript objects — for example, backgroundColor instead of background-color. Also styles do not cascade automatically, so you must pass style props to each component that needs them. A concrete example: change the color of a Text using an inline object bound to a prop. For maintainability, when styles repeat across components, refactor those objects into StyleSheet. create() which centralizes definitions and sends them to the native side efficiently. Try toggling a color value via state to see how inline styles update instantly.

keyIdea.title: Inline style rule
keyIdea.text: Inline styles are JavaScript objects inside JSX; use them for quick, dynamic styling but refactor repeating rules into StyleSheet for reuse.

content.html:
Definition

Inline Styles

Pass a JavaScript object to the style prop. Outer braces mark a JavaScript expression; inner braces form the object literal.

Best uses
  • Quick one-off adjustments while prototyping.
  • Dynamic styles based on props or state.
  • Small conditional variations that are local to a component.
Common error
Using CSS strings like "background-color: red" instead of an object with backgroundColor: 'red'.
Visual example
{`Hello

// dynamic example
Resizable text`}
Inline styles update immediately when the underlying JavaScript values change. For repeated patterns, extract style objects into a StyleSheet for clarity and performance.
Pro Tip

Use inline styles for dynamic values, then move static repeated rules into StyleSheet.create().

screens.title: StyleSheet.create() — Organizing Styles
screens.subtitle: Why centralize styles and how StyleSheet optimizes them

narration.text: StyleSheet. create() is the recommended pattern for organizing styles in React Native. You pass an object mapping style names to style objects and then reference them via styles. name. This centralizes your styling, improves readability, and provides native-side optimizations because style objects can be sent to the native layer once. In practice, start with inline styles while you iterate. When rules repeat across components, extract them into a StyleSheet and import or share the object. StyleSheet also helps catch typos because you keep style keys in one place. A typical misconception is that StyleSheet. create() magically behaves like C S S classes with inheritance; it does not. It simply returns an object whose values point to validated style identifiers. Example code from the chapter shows a styles object with container, titleText, and paragraphText. Use descriptive keys and keep style values as plain JavaScript primitives. As a concrete exercise, refactor the inline contact-row styles in a profile card into a styles. contactRow and apply it to the View. After refactoring, test that the UI still responds as before but now the style definitions are more maintainable. What repeating rules in your app would you extract first?

keyIdea.title: StyleSheet benefit
keyIdea.text: StyleSheet.create() centralizes styles, aids reuse, and lets React Native perform native-side optimizations for style objects.

content.html:
Process Flow

StyleSheet.create()

Extract repeated or static style rules into a centralized StyleSheet object for readability and performance.

Why extract styles
  • Reduces duplication and keeps components lean.
  • Helps find and fix typos in one place.
  • Enables style validation and potential native optimizations.
Refactor example
{`import { StyleSheet, Text, View, Image } from 'react-native';

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  container: { flex: 1, alignItems: 'center', justifyContent: 'center' },
  titleText: { fontSize: 24, fontWeight: 'bold', color: 'purple' },
  paragraphText: { fontSize: 16, color: 'gray', marginTop: 10 },
});

// Usage: Welcome`}
Key Takeaway

Use StyleSheet.create() to centralize static style rules, then apply them via the style prop for cleaner, faster code.

Code Walkthrough

Profile Card

Follow the chapter's example closely: container View, Image with uri, and Text nodes styled via StyleSheet.

Common pitfall
Image without width/height may not render; Text nodes must be nested inside a Text component.
Starter code (visual)

import { StyleSheet, Text, View, Image } from 'react-native';

export default function App() {

      Jane Doe

}

  container: { flex: 1, alignItems: 'center', justifyContent: 'center', padding: 20 },

screens.title: From Inline to StyleSheet — Refactor Steps
screens.subtitle: A practical refactor sequence with checks

narration.text: Refactoring inline styles into a StyleSheet is a small process with big maintainability benefits. Start by identifying repeated style objects across components, such as paddings, font sizes, or color rules. Next, create a StyleSheet. create() call and add keys for the repeating patterns. Replace the inline style prop values with references to the corresponding styles. key. After replacing, run the app and verify visual parity. If a rule was dynamic, consider keeping small inline overrides by combining style props: pass an array like [styles. base, { color: dynamicColor }]. Finally, move related styles into a shared file if multiple components need the same style definitions. A common pitfall is to blindly extract single-use inline objects; extraction is most beneficial when reuse or readability improves. Another misunderstanding is thinking that extraction changes visual behavior — it should not. Use small, incremental changes and test after each step. As a concrete check, toggle the user's fontSize in the refactored code to confirm dynamic overrides still work. Which repeated rule in your profile card would you extract first and why? From Inline to StyleSheet — Refactor Steps means identify repetition, extract keys to stylesheet.create(), replace inline uses, and verify behavior with dynamic overrides as needed.. In practical terms, a practical refactor sequence with checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor pattern
keyIdea.text: Identify repetition, extract keys to StyleSheet.create(), replace inline uses, and verify behavior with dynamic overrides as needed.

content.html:
Process Flow

Refactor Steps

1. Identify
Find repeated inline objects to extract.
2. Extract
Create keys inside StyleSheet.create().
3. Replace
Use styles.key in the style prop.
4. Verify
Run the app and confirm identical visuals and dynamic overrides.
Example merge pattern
Combine static and dynamic styles: style={[styles.baseText, { color: dynamicColor }]} so you keep both reuse and flexibility.
Key Takeaway

Refactor incrementally, verify UI parity, and use style arrays for dynamic values.

screens.title: Image Handling and Sizing
screens.subtitle: Network vs local assets, required style, and common rendering pitfalls

narration.text: Images in React Native can come from network URIs or local assets. For network images you pass an object like { uri: 'https://...' } to the source prop. For local images use require with the asset path. A frequent beginner mistake is to omit width and height; images often need explicit dimensions to render as expected because layout cannot infer natural content size across platforms. You can control shape with borderRadius and use resizeMode for fitting behavior. When using remote images, consider loading and placeholder behavior — though that is beyond this chapter, be prepared to set sensible dimensions and a fallback. A practical tip: wrap Image in a fixed-size View if you want a consistent frame, and set Image style to width: '100%' and height: '100%' with borderRadius to create a circular avatar effect. Also ensure accessibility props such as accessible and accessibilityLabel are provided for meaningful images. Try replacing the example avatar URI with your own and adjust profileImage width and height to see how layout changes. What happens if you set width only and omit height on an Image inside a flex container?

keyIdea.title: Image rules
keyIdea.text: Set explicit width and height for images, use uri for network sources, and control shape with borderRadius and resizeMode.

content.html:
Architecture

Image handling

Use uri for network images and require for local assets. Always set width and height or constrain via a parent container to ensure predictable rendering.

Best practices
  • Provide explicit dimensions or a constrained parent.
  • Use borderRadius with matching width/height for circles.
  • Use accessibilityLabel for meaningful images.
Tip
Use a placeholder while a network image loads to avoid layout jumps.
Sizing example
{`// network image


// inside constrained parent

  
`}
Key Takeaway

Give images explicit size or constrain them via parent View; use uri or require depending on source and add accessible labels.

screens.title: Common Beginner Errors & Debugging
screens.subtitle: Text placement, CSS vs JS styles, and Image sizing errors

narration.text: Beginners frequently encounter a few recurring errors when starting with React Native. First, placing raw text directly inside a View instead of wrapping it in a Text component. This often leads to runtime warnings or incorrect layout. Second, attempting to apply C S S strings rather than JavaScript objects. Remember C S S property names are camelCased in JavaScript, and the style prop expects an object. Third, forgetting to set width and height for Image components, which can prevent images from appearing. When you see these problems, the debugging path is simple: check the element types, verify style prop types, and confirm required style keys are present. Another issue is assuming style inheritance like web C S S; each component's style is independent, and text-specific styles only apply when set on Text components or passed via nested Text elements. For debugging, use console logging of props, inspect the component tree in a React Native inspector, and make small incremental changes to see immediate effects. As you practice by building the profile card, deliberately introduce one of these mistakes and then fix it — that hands-on correction helps cement the rules. Which debugging step will you try first when an Image fails to render?

keyIdea.title: Debug checklist
keyIdea.text: If UI misbehaves: ensure text is inside Text, styles are objects with camelCase keys, and images have explicit dimensions.

content.html:
Common Mistakes

Debugging checklist

  • Text nodes must be inside Text components; otherwise wrap them correctly.
  • Style prop must receive a JavaScript object or an array of objects, not a CSS string.
  • Image components need explicit width and height, or a constrained parent with percentage sizing.
Use the inspector and small edits to locate the offending node quickly. Confirm prop types and style shapes if something looks off.
Example fix
{`// Incorrect
Hello World

// Correct
Hello World`}
Key Takeaway

Small structural errors cause many beginner bugs. Check node types, style shapes, and image dimensions first.

screens.title: Activity: Build and Refactor the Profile Card
screens.subtitle: Stepwise instructions and challenge prompts

narration.text: This activity guides you from an empty App. js to a functioning profile card and then asks you to refactor styles. Start with a blank App. js and import React, View, Text, Image, and StyleSheet from react-native. First, render a View as the root container and inside it place a Text reading "Hello World" wrapped in a Text component to confirm your environment. Next, add an Image using a network URI and give it explicit width and height. Add two Text components for the name and title. At this stage you will likely use inline style objects to set color, fontSize, margin, and alignment so you can iterate quickly. After confirming the layout, create a StyleSheet. create() call and move container, profileImage, userName, and userTitle into it. Replace the inline style objects with styles. X references. Verify the app runs and visually matches the inline version. Challenge: add a conditional bio Text that only renders when a bio prop is present, and practice combining styles via an array for a dynamic color override. This hands-on refactor teaches both JSX composition and practical style organization. What small change will you make next to personalize your profile card?

keyIdea.title: Activity goal

Follow the plan: build, verify, then refactor. Incremental changes reduce errors and teach how JSX and styles interact.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three compact ideas to take forward

narration.text: Remember these three compact ideas as you continue building with React Native. First, components are the fundamental building blocks: design them small, prop-driven, and reusable so your UI composes cleanly. Second, core components have distinct roles — View for layout, Text for all textual content, and Image for images. Respect those roles to prevent common layout and rendering errors. Third, style with JavaScript objects: use inline styles for quick, dynamic values, and extract repeated rules into StyleSheet. create() for reuse and better native-side handling. These three ideas are practical guardrails that keep your code maintainable and cross-platform friendly. When you build the profile card, use them as a checklist: small component, correct node types, and organized styles. Which of the three will you focus on improving next in your code?

keyIdea.title: Memorable summary
keyIdea.text: Components + JSX + organized styles = predictable, reusable mobile UI code.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Key Concepts
Components
Independent, reusable units that encapsulate rendering and behavior.
Core components
Use View for layout, Text for all visible text, and Image for images.
Styling
Pass JavaScript objects to style; prefer StyleSheet.create() for repeated styles.
Summary Takeaway

Apply small, focused components, use the right core components, and centralize styles to build maintainable React Native apps.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three quick reminders to keep the basics correct

narration.text: A quick reference you can keep in mind while coding: always wrap visible text in Text components, always give images explicit dimensions or constrain them via a parent, and use StyleSheet. create() to organize repeated style rules. These rules prevent the most common rendering and layout problems beginners face and make your code easier to read. When you pair these small habits with small, reusable components, you will have a stable foundation to build more complex screens. As you continue, return to the profile-card exercise and iterate using these reminders until they become second nature. What to Remember means text in text, images sized, styles centralized — these simple guards reduce bugs and improve maintainability.. In practical terms, three quick reminders to keep the basics correct. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Quick reference
keyIdea.text: Text in Text, images sized, styles centralized — these simple guards reduce bugs and improve maintainability.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Quick Reference
Wrap text
Always place visible text inside a Text component to avoid errors.
Size images
Provide width and height or use a constrained parent to ensure images render.
Centralize styles
Use StyleSheet.create() for repeated rules and better native performance.
Final Thought

These simple habits keep your React Native UIs predictable, accessible, and easy to maintain as your app grows.
